u.src: Now Daiyu had the woman from Baochai's household shown in, exchanged greetings with her, and received the letter she presented.
Daiyu told her to go and have some tea, then opened Baochai's letter and read the following:

p.src: Your younger sister was born beneath an ill-starred fate; our family's fortunes have been beset by hardship, we sisters are left forlorn, and our aged mother is failing. Moreover, snarls and savage words rage without cease from dawn till dusk. Then cruel calamity and unforeseen disaster descended upon us, like a sudden gale and driving rain. I toss and turn deep into the night; how can I endure this burden of sorrow? Since our hearts are one, how could you not feel compassion for all this? I recall when we founded the Crab-Flower Club: it was clear autumn, and as we admired chrysanthemums and held crabs in hand, our fellowship was joyous and warm. I still remember the lines, “Proud and aloof from the world—with whom shall you hide? Your flowers bloom like all the rest—why then so late?” I cannot recall them without sighing that we two, too, are like those chaste blossoms that leave their fragrance behind in the cold. Stirred by these memories, I have composed four stanzas. They are no idle moaning without cause, but rather long songs sung in place of weeping. I grieve at the ceaseless passing of the seasons—once more it is clear autumn. I lament the misfortunes that have befallen my house, and dwell alone with the sorrows of parting. In the northern hall my mother remains—yet how can the daylily banish sorrow? Nothing can dispel my grief; my heart trembles in distress. First stanza. Clouds mass heavily, and the autumn wind blows bitter; I pace the courtyard where frost-dried leaves lie. Where shall I go, and what path shall I follow, now that I have lost the joys of old? In stillness I ponder it, and anguish pierces my heart! Second stanza. The sturgeon has its deep pool, and the crane its fish-weir. The scaled creatures lie hidden below, while the feathered ones spread their wings afar! I scratch my head and question the boundless void: beneath high heaven and upon the broad earth, who understands my everlasting pain? Third stanza. The Silver River gleams as the cold steals in; moonbeams slant across the night while the jade water-clock sinks low. My burning sorrow draws forth a mournful song; I sing and sing again, sending it to the one who knows my heart. Fourth stanza.

p.src: After reading the letter, Daiyu was overcome with sorrow. Then she thought, “Cousin Bao sent this to no one but me. It is surely because one discerning soul cherishes another.” As she sat lost in thought, she heard someone outside ask, “Is Cousin Lin at home?” Folding up Baochai's letter, Daiyu called back, “Who is it?” Even as she asked, several young ladies entered: Tanchun, Xiangyun, Li Wen, and Li Qi. After exchanging greetings, they drank the tea Xueyan poured and chatted about one thing and another. When the chrysanthemum poems of the year before last came to mind, Daiyu said, “Since Cousin Bao moved out, she has visited twice, but now she no longer comes even when something is happening. It really is strange. I wonder whether she will ever come back to us.” Tanchun smiled faintly. “Why wouldn't she? She is bound to come sooner or later. It is only that her honored sister-in-law is rather difficult, Aunt Xue is growing old, and then there is Cousin Xue's affair. Naturally Cousin Bao must see to everything. How could she have as much leisure as before?” While they were speaking, a sudden rush of wind sent a host of fallen leaves rattling against the paper window. After a little while, a waft of pure fragrance drifted in. Catching the scent, they all exclaimed, “Where is this fragrant breeze coming from? What sort of fragrance does it resemble?” “It seems like sweet osmanthus,” said Daiyu. Tanchun laughed. “Cousin Lin, you never can rid yourself of southern ways of speaking. At this late point in the ninth month, how could there still be osmanthus blossoms?” Daiyu laughed. “Quite so. Otherwise, why didn't I simply say it was osmanthus, instead of saying it merely seemed like it?” Xiangyun said, “Third Cousin, you shouldn't be so sure. Don't you remember, ‘Lotus blossoms for ten leagues, and osmanthus in the third month of autumn’? In the south, this is precisely when the late osmanthus blooms. You simply have never seen it. When you go south one day, you will naturally understand.” Tanchun laughed. “What reason would I have to go south? Besides, I knew that long ago; I have no need of your boasting.” Li Wen and Li Qi merely smiled behind pursed lips. Daiyu said, “Little sister, no one can say for certain. As the saying goes, ‘People are immortals who roam the earth.’ One may be here today and no one knows where tomorrow. Take me, for example: I am from the south, so how did I come to be here?” Xiangyun clapped her hands and laughed. “Third Cousin has been stumped by Cousin Lin today! Not only did Cousin Lin come here from the south, but even among those of us gathered here, no two are quite alike. Some are native northerners; some have southern roots but were born and raised in the north; and some were born and raised in the south before coming north. Yet today we have all gathered in one place.

p.src: It shows that everyone has a destiny, and that places and people are each bound by their own affinities.” Everyone nodded on hearing this, while Tanchun merely smiled. After chatting a while longer, they all took their leave. Daiyu accompanied them to the door, but they all said, “You have only just begun to recover. Don't come outside and risk catching a chill.” So Daiyu remained in the doorway, talking and exchanging a few more warm courtesies with the four of them, then watched as they left the courtyard. She went back in and sat down. By now the woodland birds were returning to the hills and the setting sun was sinking in the west. Xiangyun's talk of the south set her thinking: “If my parents were still alive, I would be amid the southern scenery—flowers in spring and moonlit nights in autumn, limpid waters and lovely hills, the Twenty-Four Bridges, and the relics of the Six Dynasties. There would be no lack of servants to attend me; I could do as I pleased in all things and speak without reserve. With perfumed carriages and painted pleasure-boats, red apricot blossoms and blue wine-shop banners, I would be mistress of all around me. But today I live beneath another's roof. Though I am shown every consideration, there is nowhere and nothing in which I need not be mindful of myself. What sin can I have committed in a former life, to be so lonely and desolate in this one? It is truly as the Last Ruler Li said: ‘Here, every day, I do nothing but wash my face with tears!’” As these thoughts passed through her mind, her spirit wandered far away before she knew it.

p.src: Zijuan came over and, seeing her in this state, guessed that the recent talk of south and north must have touched upon Daiyu’s private sorrow. She therefore asked, “The young ladies have been talking with you for quite a while; I expect you have tired yourself again. Just now I had Xueyan tell the kitchen to make you a bowl of cured-ham and cabbage soup, with a little dried shrimp, tender bamboo shoot, and laver. Do you think you might like it?” “Very well,” said Daiyu. “We have also cooked a little glutinous-rice porridge,” said Zijuan. Daiyu nodded and added, “You two should have cooked that porridge yourselves instead of having the kitchen do it.” “I was afraid the kitchen might not prepare it cleanly,” said Zijuan, “so we are cooking it ourselves. Even about the soup, I told Xueyan and Cook Liu to make sure everything was clean. Cook Liu said she would see to everything, then take it to her own room and have her daughter Wuer watch it simmer.” “It is not that I think other people dirty,” said Daiyu. “It is only that I have been ill for so many days, and whenever anything has been lacking or overlooked, others have had to attend to it. And now, ordering first soup and then porridge, I am sure to make a nuisance of myself.” As she spoke, her eyes reddened once more. “You are worrying too much, miss,” said Zijuan. You are the Old Lady’s granddaughter through her daughter, and the darling of her heart besides. Others would dearly love the chance to please you and cannot even get it—how could anyone complain?” Daiyu nodded, then asked, “This Wuer you just mentioned—is she not the girl who was with Fangguan from Master Bao’s apartments that day?” “That is she,” said Zijuan. “Did I not hear that she was to enter service here?” asked Daiyu. “Indeed. She fell ill, and by the time she recovered and was ready to come, the trouble involving Qingwen and the others had just broken out, so the matter was delayed.” “As I recall, she was a rather neat and presentable girl,” said Daiyu. As she spoke, an old servant woman brought the soup from outside. When Xueyan went out to receive it, the woman said, “Cook Liu asks me to tell you, miss, that her Wuer made this. She dared not prepare it in the main kitchen, for fear you might find it unclean.” Xueyan acknowledged her and carried it inside. Daiyu had already heard from within and instructed Xueyan to tell the old woman, when she went back, that Cook Liu had been most thoughtful. Xueyan went out and delivered the message, and the old woman departed. Xueyan then set Daiyu’s bowl and chopsticks on a small table and asked, “We still have some five-spice kohlrabi we brought from the south. Shall I dress some with sesame oil and vinegar?” “That will do,” said Daiyu, “but do not put yourself to needless trouble.”

p.src: The porridge was served, and Daiyu ate half a bowl. She took two spoonfuls of soup, then set it aside. The two maids cleared everything away, wiped the small table clean and carried it out, then replaced it with the table normally kept there. After rinsing her mouth and washing her hands, Daiyu asked, “Zijuan, have you replenished the incense?” “I shall do it now,” said Zijuan. “You two eat the soup and porridge,” said Daiyu. “They taste quite good, and they are clean besides. I shall replenish the incense myself.” The two assented and went to eat in the outer room.

p.src: Daiyu replenished the incense and sat alone. Just as she was about to pick up a book, she heard the wind in the garden rushing straight from west to east, sweeping through the branches and setting them rustling and clattering without cease. Presently the iron wind chimes beneath the eaves also began jangling wildly and incessantly. Before long Xueyan, who had finished eating first, came in to attend her. Daiyu asked, “The weather has turned cold. The other day I told you to air those light fur garments. Have you done so?” “They have all been aired,” said Xueyan. “Bring me one to put around my shoulders,” said Daiyu. Xueyan went and brought back a bundle of light fur garments. She opened the felt wrapping and let Daiyu choose one herself. Among them lay a small silk-wrapped bundle. Daiyu reached out, picked it up, and opened it. Inside were the old handkerchiefs Baoyu had sent her during his illness, still bearing the poems she herself had written and the stains of her tears. Wrapped within them were the cut-up fragrance pouch and fan case, together with the tassel from Baoyu’s Precious Jade of Spiritual Understanding. They had been taken from the chest when the clothes were aired, and Zijuan, afraid they might be lost, had tucked them into this felt wrapping. Once Daiyu saw them, she forgot all about choosing a garment. Holding the two handkerchiefs in her hands, she stared blankly at the poems she had written long ago. After gazing at them for a while, she could not keep her tears from falling in a steady stream. Zijuan had just come in from the outer room when she saw Xueyan standing dumbfounded to one side, holding a felt-wrapped bundle of clothes. On the small table lay the slashed fragrance pouch, two or three pieces of the fan case, and the severed tassel, while Daiyu held the two old, inscribed handkerchiefs in her hands and wept over them. As the verse says:

p.src: Seeing her like this, Zijuan knew that the sight of those things had stirred Daiyu's sorrow and awakened memories of the past. Realizing that advice would be useless, she could only smile and say, “Why do you still look at those things, miss? They are merely relics of the little scenes Second Master Bao and you made in those childhood years, when you were friends one moment and angry with each other the next. If you had treated each other then with the courtesy and respect you show now, how could these things ever have been needlessly spoiled?” Zijuan had meant these words to cheer Daiyu, but instead they recalled even more vividly the old days between Daiyu and Baoyu when she had first arrived, and her pearly tears streamed all the faster. Zijuan urged her again, “Xueyan is waiting here, miss. Do put something on.” Only then did Daiyu set down the handkerchief. Zijuan hastily picked it up, wrapped the perfume sachet and the other things together, and took them away. Daiyu then put on a fur-lined garment and went out gloomily to sit in the outer room. Glancing back, she saw that Baochai's poetic letter still lay unput away on the table. She took it up and read it twice more, then sighed, “Our circumstances differ, but our sorrow is the same. I may as well compose four stanzas too and set them to qin notation, so that they may be both played and sung. Tomorrow I shall write them out and send them to her as my answering composition.” She told Xueyan to bring the brush and inkstone from the table outside, dipped her brush in ink, and swiftly composed four stanzas. Then she took out her qin scores and borrowed the melodies of the two pieces “Secluded Orchid” and “Longing for the Worthy,” adapting their notes and rhythms to fit what she had written. When all was properly matched, she copied it out, ready to send to Baochai. She immediately told Xueyan to take from the chest the small qin she had brought with her, then tuned its strings and practised the fingering. Daiyu was exceptionally intelligent by nature and had studied the instrument for a time in the south. Though her hands were out of practice, once she reviewed the principles, her skill quickly returned. After she had played for a while, the night was already deep, so she told Zijuan to put everything away and prepare for bed. But of this no more.

p.src: Now Baoyu rose that morning, washed and dressed, and was on his way to the schoolroom with Beiming when Moyu came running up to meet him, grinning. “You're in luck today, Second Master! The old master isn't in the schoolroom, so everyone has been given the day off.” “Is that really true?” asked Baoyu. Moyu replied, “If you don't believe me, Second Master, aren't those Third Master and young Master Lan coming now?” Baoyu looked and saw Jia Huan and Jia Lan approaching with their pages, both smiling and chattering away about something or other. When they saw Baoyu, they stopped and stood respectfully with their hands lowered. Baoyu asked, “Why have you two come back so soon?” Jia Huan answered, “The old master has business today. He said we were to have one day off and return tomorrow.” Only after hearing this did Baoyu turn back to report the matter to Grandmother Jia and Jia Zheng, after which he returned to Happy Red Court. Xiren asked, “Why have you come back again?” Baoyu told her what had happened. He sat only a little while before starting for the door. “Where are you going in such a hurry?” Xiren asked. Even though lessons have been cancelled, if you ask me, you ought to rest and restore your spirits.” Baoyu stopped, lowered his head, and said, “What you say is true. But it is so rare to get a day off. If I cannot even go out and relax, you really ought to take a little pity on me.” Hearing how pitifully he spoke, Xiren laughed and said, “Then do as you please, young master.” Just as they were speaking, his meal was brought in. Baoyu could do nothing but eat first. He hurriedly finished in a few mouthfuls, rinsed his mouth, and flew off like a wisp of smoke to Daiyu's rooms.

Jia Huan answered, “The old master has business today. He said we were to have one day off and return tomorrow.”
Only after hearing this did Baoyu turn back to report the matter to Grandmother Jia and Jia Zheng, after which he returned to Happy Red Court.
Xiren asked, “Why have you come back again?”
Baoyu told her what had happened. He sat only a little while before starting for the door.
“Where are you going in such a hurry?” Xiren asked.
Even though lessons have been cancelled, if you ask me, you ought to rest and restore your spirits.”
Baoyu stopped, lowered his head, and said, “What you say is true.
But it is so rare to get a day off. If I cannot even go out and relax, you really ought to take a little pity on me.”
Hearing how pitifully he spoke, Xiren laughed and said, “Then do as you please, young master.”
Just as they were speaking, his meal was brought in.
Baoyu could do nothing but eat first. He hurriedly finished in a few mouthfuls, rinsed his mouth, and flew off like a wisp of smoke to Daiyu's rooms.

p.src: When he reached the doorway, he saw Xueyan in the courtyard hanging silk handkerchiefs out to dry. Baoyu asked her, “Has your mistress eaten?” Xueyan replied, “She drank half a bowl of congee early this morning, but had no appetite for a meal. She is dozing just now. Please go and walk somewhere else for a while, Second Master, and come back later.” Baoyu had no choice but to turn back.

p.src: With nowhere else to go, he suddenly remembered that he had not seen Xichun for several days, so he wandered over to Smartweed Breeze Lodge. He had just reached the window when he noticed that all was perfectly still, without a human voice. Baoyu supposed that she too was taking an afternoon nap and thought it improper to go inside. Just as he was about to leave, he heard a faint sound from inside, though he could not tell what it was. Baoyu stopped to listen. After quite a while, there came another sharp click. Before he had identified it, he heard someone say, “I have played a stone here. Shouldn't you answer over there?” Baoyu then realized that they were playing Go, but he could not immediately recognize the speaker's voice. Next he heard Xichun say, “What is there to fear? If you capture me this way, I answer this way; then you capture me like this, and I answer like that. I still have a move in reserve, and in the end my stones will connect.” The other person said, “And what if I capture this way?” “Ah!” cried Xichun. “There is a snapback hidden in it! I failed to guard against that.” Listening, Baoyu found the other voice very familiar, yet it belonged to none of his sisters. Thinking there could be no outsider in Xichun's room, he gently raised the curtain and went in. When he looked, he saw that it was none other than Miaoyu of Green Bower Hermitage, the self-styled Outsider Beyond the Threshold. Seeing that it was Miaoyu, Baoyu did not dare disturb her. Miaoyu and Xichun were both deep in thought and took no notice of him. Baoyu stood beside them and watched how the two played. He saw Miaoyu lower her head and ask Xichun, “Are you going to abandon this corner group?” “Of course not,” said Xichun. “All your stones in there are dead. What have I to fear?” Miaoyu said, “Do not boast too soon. Let us see.” Xichun said, “Then I shall start the attack and see what you can do.” Miaoyu smiled faintly, connected a stone along the edge, then turned back to capture. In this way she took the whole of Xichun's corner group, and said with a smile, “This is called the ‘Upside-Down Boot’ formation.”

p.src: Before Xichun could answer, Baoyu, unable to contain himself at her side, burst out laughing and gave them both a terrible fright. Xichun said, “What do you mean by this? You came in without saying a word and played such a mischievous trick to frighten us. When did you come in?” Baoyu replied, “I came in a while ago and have been watching you two dispute over that corner move.” As he spoke, he bowed to Miaoyu and then asked with a smile, “Reverend Miaoyu seldom leaves the seclusion of her convent. What brings you down to the mortal world today?” At this, Miaoyu suddenly blushed. Without replying, she lowered her head and looked at the game. Realizing that he had been forward, Baoyu hastily smiled apologetically. “Those who have renounced the world are indeed unlike worldly people such as us. Above all, their hearts are tranquil. From tranquility comes spiritual perception, and from perception comes wisdom.” Before Baoyu had finished, Miaoyu slightly raised her eyes and glanced at him, then lowered her head again as a blush gradually spread across her face. Seeing that she ignored him, Baoyu could only sit down awkwardly beside them. Xichun wanted to continue the game, but after a long silence Miaoyu said, “Let us play again another time.” She rose, straightened her clothes, sat down again, and asked Baoyu dreamily, “Where have you come from?” Baoyu had been longing for such an opening so that he might explain his earlier remark, but suddenly thought, “Perhaps this is one of Miaoyu’s Zen challenges.” His face reddened in turn, and he could find no answer. Miaoyu smiled faintly and turned to speak with Xichun. Xichun also laughed. “Second Brother, what is so difficult about answering that? Haven’t you heard the common saying, ‘I come from where I came’?” Is that worth blushing over? You look as though you had met a stranger.” Hearing this, Miaoyu thought of herself. Her heart stirred and her face grew hot; knowing that she too must be blushing, she began to feel embarrassed. She therefore stood and said, “I have been here a long while. I must return to the convent.” Xichun knew Miaoyu’s temperament and did not press her to stay, but escorted her to the door. Miaoyu said with a smile, “I have not been here for so long, and the paths wind about so much that I may lose my way back.” Baoyu said, “Then how would it be if I showed you the way?” Miaoyu replied, “I would not presume to ask it. After you, Second Master.” The two took leave of Xichun and departed from Smartweed Breeze Lodge. Following the winding paths, they drew near the Naiad’s House and suddenly heard the resonant notes of strings. Miaoyu asked, “Where is that qin music coming from?” Baoyu replied, “I expect Cousin Lin is playing the qin in her quarters.” Miaoyu said, “So she can play this too. Why have I never heard it mentioned before?” Baoyu told her all about Daiyu’s circumstances, then said, “Let us go and see her.”

p.src: Miaoyu listened, then paled in astonishment. “Why has the melody suddenly shifted into the altered zhi mode? Its resonance is powerful enough to split metal and stone. But it is too intense.” “What will happen if it is too intense?” Baoyu asked. “I fear it cannot last,” Miaoyu replied. While they were still discussing it, the principal string snapped with a twang. Miaoyu rose and hurried away. “What does it mean?” Baoyu asked. “You will learn in time. There is no need for you to say anything more,” Miaoyu replied. And with that, she left. Baoyu was left full of doubts and returned dejectedly to Happy Red Court. We shall say no more of him. As for Miaoyu, when she returned, a Taoist matron was already there to receive her. After the convent gate had been shut, she sat for a while and recited the Daily Offices of the Chan School from beginning to end. After supper, she lit incense and bowed before the Bodhisattva, then told the Taoist matron to retire. Her meditation couch and backrest had already been arranged; she stilled her breath, lowered the curtain, and sat cross-legged, seeking to banish delusive thoughts and approach true suchness. After the third watch, she heard tiles clattering across the roof. Fearing a thief had come, Miaoyu stepped down from her meditation couch and went out to the front veranda, where she saw cloud shadows stretching across the sky and moonlight flowing like water. The weather was not yet very cold. After standing alone by the railing for a while, she suddenly heard two cats on the roof calling to each other in turns. Miaoyu suddenly recalled what Baoyu had said that day, and before she knew it her heart was pounding and her ears were burning. She hastily gathered her thoughts, returned to the meditation room, and seated herself once more upon the couch. But her spirit would not remain composed. All at once it was as if ten thousand horses were galloping through her mind; the meditation couch seemed to pitch and sway, and she felt herself no longer within the convent. A host of princes and young noblemen appeared, each seeking her hand, while matchmakers tugged and pulled at her, trying to help her into a carriage, though she refused to go. Then robbers came to abduct her, threatening her with knives and cudgels, until she could only weep and cry out for help. Her cries had already awakened all the nuns and Taoist matrons in the convent, who brought lamps to see what was happening. They saw Miaoyu with both arms flung wide and froth running from her mouth. When they urgently tried to wake her, her eyes were staring rigidly and both cheeks were bright red. She cursed them: “The Bodhisattva protects me! What do you villains think you can do to me?” Everyone was so frightened that they did not know what to do. “We are all here with you,” they said. “Please wake up!” “I want to go home,” said Miaoyu. “Find some decent person to escort me back.” “But this is the room where you live,” the Taoist matron told her. As she spoke, she told another nun to hurry before Guanyin and pray. They drew a divination slip and consulted the book, which said that Miaoyu had offended a female spirit in the southwest corner. “That must be it,” one of them said. No one has ever lived in the southwest corner of Prospect Garden, so there must indeed be a baleful presence there.” Meanwhile, they bustled about preparing broth and water for her.

p.src: The nun had originally accompanied Miaoyu from the south and naturally tended her more devotedly than the others. She stayed close beside Miaoyu and sat on the meditation couch. Miaoyu turned to her. “Who are you?” “It is I,” replied the nun. Miaoyu looked closely at her. “So it is you.” She threw her arms around the nun and began sobbing bitterly. “You are my mother! If you do not save me, I shall not live!” The nun kept calling her back to her senses while rubbing and soothing her. p.src: The nun sent someone to summon physicians to take Miaoyu's pulse. One said that worry had injured her spleen; another, that heat had entered the chamber of the blood; another, that an evil spirit had assailed her; and still another, that she had caught a chill both internally and externally. No firm conclusion was reached. Later another physician was brought in. After examining her, he asked, “Has she ever practiced seated meditation?” “She has always practiced it,” replied the Taoist matron. “Did this illness come on suddenly last night?” the physician asked. “Yes,” said the Taoist matron. “It was caused by demonic delusion arising during meditation,” said the physician. “Is it dangerous?” everyone asked. “Fortunately, she had not been meditating for long, so the demonic influence has not penetrated deeply. She can still be saved,” replied the physician. He prescribed medicine to subdue the fire of the heart. After one dose, she grew somewhat calmer. When the idle young rakes outside heard what had happened, they invented all manner of rumors. “How could anyone of her age endure such restraint? Besides, with such alluring looks and such a clever, sensitive nature, who knows into whose hands she will eventually fly, and who will be the lucky man to profit by it?” Several days passed. Though Miaoyu's illness improved a little, her faculties had not fully recovered, and she remained somewhat dazed.
